claims.text: Depositing a ZrC-modified protective coating on boride-based components will improve their resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion relative to uncoated components.
Chemical vapor deposition or sputtering can be used to form a dense ZrC-modified coating on the boride surface.
The deposited coating will adhere well to the underlying boride substrate.
ZrC modification can reduce coating defects.
ZrC is a high-temperature ceramic material with good chemical stability.
ZrC has high thermal stability under molten-aluminum exposure conditions.
A dense ZrC-containing layer will act as a barrier to aluminum diffusion into the boride substrate.
The ZrC-containing layer will impede chemical reaction between molten aluminum and the boride substrate.
Impeded diffusion and reaction will reduce corrosion and structural degradation of the boride component.
ZrC addition has improved corrosion resistance in a Ni-P nanocomposite coating on N80 steel.
The ZrC-coated boride component will have significantly less corrosion depth than an uncoated component under equivalent molten-aluminum exposure.
The ZrC-coated boride component will have significantly less weight loss than an uncoated component under equivalent molten-aluminum exposure.
The ZrC-coated boride component will show less microstructural degradation than an uncoated component under equivalent molten-aluminum exposure.
Temperatures around or above 660 degrees Celsius are representative of hot-dip aluminum-plating exposure.
The corrosion benefit will persist if the coating retains uniform thickness, adhesion, and freedom from significant defects during thermal and mechanical cycling.
Wear or thermal-cycling damage to the coating may diminish its corrosion-protection benefit.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in corrosion indicators relative to the uncoated control would falsify the hypothesis.
